articles.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
articles.summary: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
articles.body:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was " way more awesome than people realise " in March, and called it the " best product Tesla has ever made to date " in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019 , while it was still in development.

In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.

Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something " straight out of Blade Runner ".

But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it " ugly as sin ".

Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.

"We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".

In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

articles.title: Indian-American DOJ civil rights chief  Harmeet Dhillon resigns after GOP midterm setback
articles.summary: Harmeet K Dhillon, a prominent Indian-American lawyer and civil rights chief under Trump, resigns from the DOJ following Republican midterm setbacks, highlighting her controversial enforcement shifts and investigations into diversity and university policies.
articles.body: Harmeet K Dhillon, an Indian-American lawyer who led a major shift in the US Justice Department's civil rights enforcement priorities under President Donald Trump, has resigned from her position, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Thursday.Dhillon's departure comes two days after Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections. She is among the first senior officials to leave the administration following the Republican losses.As head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Dhillon oversaw changes to an agency traditionally responsible for enforcing voting rights protections and investigating racial discrimination. Under her leadership, the division redirected its attention towards challenging diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes, examining alleged antisemitism on university campuses and pursuing cases involving gun rights.The shift triggered departures among career attorneys, several of whom left the division amid disagreements over its new direction. Dhillon had accused some of the lawyers of prioritising liberal causes and resisting the Trump administration's policies.In her resignation letter, Dhillon highlighted the administration's efforts to challenge diversity programmes and school policies concerning transgender students as achievements during her tenure. She also claimed credit for changes to women's sports policies, as per Reuters."We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more," she wrote on X while thanking Trump for appointing her.Dhillon had informed the White House in October that she intended to step down, according to her resignation letter. She is expected to return to her law firm, The Dhillon Law Group, a spokesperson said.However, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters that her decision was also influenced by frustration over being overlooked for promotions within the Justice Department. They said she wanted to return to private practice and rebuild her firm, which had recently lost several attorneys to other practices.University probes and voter data disputesShe also led investigations involving several prominent American universities, with inquiries focusing on alleged antisemitism, diversity initiatives and policies concerning transgender people. The probe resulted in settlement agreements worth hundreds of millions of dollars with some institutions and contributed to the resignation of the University of Virginia's president.Harvard University, one of the administration's prominent targets, rejected a large settlement demand and repeatedly challenged the federal government in court.The division also became involved in the administration's efforts to obtain voter information from states ahead of the midterm elections. The Trump administration argued that the measures were necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting, although independent reviews have found such voting to be exceedingly rare.The Justice Department lost several legal challenges seeking access to private voter records from states. It also deployed around 1,000 staff members to monitor polling locations during Tuesday's elections.Cases involving Trump criticsDhillon's tenure included cases involving individuals the Trump administration viewed as political opponents. The division pursued a high-profile criminal case against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others accused of disrupting a church service in January during a protest against the administration's immigration enforcement operations in Minnesota.It also unsuccessfully sought criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide who testified before Congress about Trump's conduct on January 6, 2021, when supporters of the then-president stormed the US Capitol.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, has secured a major legal victory after an appeals court ruled that the city can continue implementing its
articles.body: Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, has secured a major legal victory after an appeals court ruled that the city can continue implementing its controversial tax on high-value second homes, rejecting a lower court decision that had temporarily thrown the programme into doubt. The latest ruling marks the first significant courtroom win for Mamdani's signature campaign promises to "tax the rich" and comes amid criticism from homeowners who argued that the city's rollout of the levy created confusion and unfairly targeted property owners. As reported by the New York Times, appellate court panel in Brooklyn reversed a September ruling that had ordered the city to restart the implementation process.Zohran Mamdani responds to criticsThe mayor welcomed the decision and framed it as a victory for his broader agenda of asking wealthy property owners to contribute more toward city finances.“From Day 1, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city,” Mamdani said in a statement following the ruling. The court's decision is likely to be seen as a message to critics, including homeowners upset that properties with market values exceeding the threshold could be subject to the tax. Supporters of the measure argue that owners of expensive second homes benefit from the city's services and infrastructure and should contribute more, particularly as New York grapples with budget pressures.What the tax coversGov. Kathy Hochul unveiled the tax in the spring with Mamdani’s support, and it passed in the state budget. It falls on people who live outside the city most of the time but own a high-value home there. It is a surcharge on property tax bills and applies to:* condos and co-ops used as second homes with a “market value,” set by the city’s Finance Department, of at least $1 million* one-, two- and three-family second homes with a market value above $5 millionThe tax does not apply if the home is rented out or a relative of the owner lives there most of the time. It is expected to raise about $500 million a year for the city.What the lawsuit was aboutThe suit did not challenge the legality of the tax. It argued that the city caused confusion by sending notices to about 17,000 New Yorkers saying their properties might be subject to the tax, without first checking that the owners were not full-time residents. It also objected to the city publishing an online list of nearly one million “properties that may be subject to the charge,” with owners’ names. The city says it followed the law that created the tax.The notices asked owners to provide proof of residency, such as a driver’s licence, or a lease showing the home was rented. As of October 28, the city had approved around 8,800 applications from owners who said they were primary residents and should not be taxed. The city says it is still confident of raising the expected $500 million a year.More legal challenges aheadTwo other lawsuits seek to overturn the tax itself. Both argue that the law violates state constitutional limits on how much the city can collect in real estate taxes each year. They also say the tax is discriminatory under the US Constitution because it applies only to residents of other states.One was filed in September by former Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, his wife Hilary Geary Ross and casino mogul Steve Wynn, who live in Florida and own second homes in the city. City notices cited in the suit say the Rosses would owe about $83,000 a year and Wynn about $183,000. The other was brought by the corporation that owns the Montclair, an Upper East Side co-op building, along with several homeowners, including some from Florida and Suffolk County. articles.title: EC gives voters excluded from draft electoral rolls in 7 states another chance to apply
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) on Friday announced that voters excluded from the draft electoral rolls during the ongoing Special Intensive
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) on Friday announced that voters excluded from the draft electoral rolls during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise in seven states will be given another opportunity to have their names included in the final electoral rolls.The directive applies to electors who were issued enumeration forms but were left out of the draft rolls after being categorised as Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate (ASDD). The seven states covered are Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland.The EC has also directed officials to put in place a monitoring mechanism to ensure that no eligible voter is denied the opportunity to be included in the final electoral rolls, while simultaneously preventing duplicate enrolments."In cases where such an elector who was marked as ASDD and consequently whose name does not appear in the draft electoral roll, has shifted the place of residence within the state, such elector is not required to submit Form-8, instead he/she shall submit enumeration form along with the statement enclosed herewith as Annexure-C (indicating the new address and the assembly constituency)," the EC said in a statement.The poll body also clarified that electors who have already submitted Form-6 for fresh enrolment during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise need not submit the enumeration form and accompanying statement again. Their applications will be processed in accordance with the Commission's clarification dated November 3."Partially filled enumeration forms in respect of all such ASDD electors would be generated afresh in ERO dashboard in ECINET. The DEOs/EROs shall make all possible efforts to contact such electors through the concerned Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and ensure delivery of the enumeration forms either physically or through electronic means such as WhatsApp, e-mail or SMS, wherever contact details are available," the Commission stated.The EC further directed BLOs to coordinate with Booth Level Agents (BLAs) of various political parties to reach out to the affected electors. This would include house-to-house visits, enquiries with neighbours, family members and Resident Welfare Associations (RWAs), as well as contacting voters through available phone numbers wherever feasible.(With agency inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump says he met with Putin envoy, sees Ukraine deal soon
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he met privately on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy after the Russian official appeared with representatives from Ukraine at a White House event organized by first lady Melania Trump.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said he met privately on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy after the Russian official appeared with representatives from Ukraine at a White House event organized by first lady Melania Trump. Trump would not disclose what he discussed with Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev but predicted a deal could emerge soon aimed at resolving the Russian war in Ukraine. A U.S. delegation is scheduled to mediate talks in Abu Dhabi November 10 to 11 between representatives from Russia and Ukraine. Trump, speaking to reporters at the White House, said the war was close to being settled and that ending it might involve all of Europe. “It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine ... I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled,” Trump said. Trump has frequently predicted an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War Two was close. However, negotiations have picked up in recent weeks. Trump said he did not meet with the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday. Trump envoy Jared Kushner said U.S. officials meeting in Brussels on Thursday held “productive and substantive discussions” with Ukraine, NATO and European partners on security guarantees for Ukraine and a broader European security architecture. Kushner said in a social media post that negotiators were exploring five principal goals: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability. “Any arrangements must fully respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independent decision-making of every nation,” Kushner said. “Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another’s sovereign choices. “NATO will remain central to European collective defense, and this initiative would build upon existing institutions and commitments.” Dmitriev was among the officials at the rare face-to-face event with Ukrainian representatives at the White House to mark a six-day ceasefire that Melania Trump helped broker in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky. The deal expired on Sunday. “We have chosen humanity over war,” the first lady said at the event. “We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people.” Melania Trump said she was “involved in every stage of the planning” of the temporary ceasefire, including reviewing aerial images and assessing roadways and hospital access. President Trump, who did not attend the event, has lauded his wife’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire, telling reporters in October that “she does better than our professionals.” Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamia and Dmytro Lubinets, the country’s human rights ombudsman, also attended the event. They urged Slovenian-born Melania Trump to keep up her peace efforts. Both sides presented the first lady with thank-you gifts. Russia’s Dmitriev gave her a drawing of pink hearts from an Oleshky girl and said the child “chose to live with her family in Russia,” nodding to the fight over displaced Ukrainian children in Russia. “I love Melania,” the drawing read. The Ukrainians presented the first lady with a state award “for your brave heart, for saving our people, and for returning back Ukrainian children.” She handed the visiting delegations letters addressed to Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The visit marked the first in-person contact between Russian and US officials since Tuesday’s midterm elections, when Democrats ousted Republicans from control of Congress in a blow to Trump. The Democratic majority in Congress starting in January is widely expected to push for more aid for Ukraine and to question the Republican president’s decisions to strike a diesel deal with Russia and ease some sanctions on Moscow. Trump has increased his criticism of Zelenskyy in recent weeks. The Kremlin has said it hopes Trump will continue his peacemaking efforts despite the Republican Party’s defeat. It has also said preparations were under way for a meeting of Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China’s southern city of Shenzhen this month. Dmitriev previously met with Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, in the White House in 2025. Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, did not invite any Russian officials to the White House. Dmitriev has been involved in facilitating the release of American detainees in Russia, the reunification of Ukrainian children with their families, and the humanitarian operation in Oleshky.

articles.title: 'She killed herself, I put her body in trash can': Indian-origin Naresh Bhatt's testimony on wife's death in US
articles.summary: Indian-origin Naresh Bhatt, who is facing trial for the alleged murder of his wife Mamta Kafle in the US state of Virginia, testified on Thursday (local
articles.body: Indian-origin Naresh Bhatt, who is facing trial for the alleged murder of his wife Mamta Kafle in the US state of Virginia, testified on Thursday (local time) that she had died by suicide and that he later dismembered and disposed of her body in household trash cans. Bhatt, whose wife disappeared in July 2024 and whose body has never been found, made the claims during his second day of testimony in a murder trial in Manassas Park.Bhatt told the court that he discovered Kafle lying unresponsive on the floor of their bedroom around 4am on July 30, 2024, after waking up to attend to their infant daughter. He claimed she had vomit on her body and the floor, with pills and a bottle of medication nearby. He also alleged that open containers of pesticides were present and that the chemical appeared to be mixed with the vomit.According to his testimony, Bhatt tried to revive his wife for around 45 minutes to an hour before moving her from the bedroom to the bathroom and attempting to give her water. He claimed she remained unresponsive and was not breathing.When his defence lawyer asked why he had not called emergency services, Bhatt said he was scared and panicked. "I really at that point scared. I don't know why I did not. I tried to call. I really scared. I don't know why. Something take over me. I was really, really panic. I don't know … I don't really even, like, it's been, like, over two years. I have completed more than 3,500 hours of meditation. Still I don't have that answer," he told the court.What Bhatt saidBhatt also admitted that he had cut up his wife's body and disposed of it in trash cans at their home over the following day to day-and-a-half.He testified that after discovering Kafle's body, he contacted the couple's babysitter and took their daughter to her home. He then went to a Home Depot store, where he bought gloves and looked for items to conceal the body. Asked by his lawyer why he had purchased gloves, he replied, "I have no idea."Describing what he did after returning home, Bhatt told the court, "Put in the trash can." He added, "Reduced the size and then put in the trash can. With a, in the bag."When asked how he had done this, he said, "I had a saw. I used the saw." He also acknowledged using knives, but said, "Little bit, but not a lot," NBC Washington quoted him as saying.Prosecution challenges his version of eventsBhatt's testimony marks a major shift from what he had told police and the media after his wife's disappearance. At the time, he had claimed that Kafle had left their home and suggested she could be in New York or Texas.During cross-examination, prosecutor Matthew Sweet confronted him over the change in his account, calling him a liar. Bhatt responded, "Yes," when asked whether he had lied.The prosecution had earlier presented surveillance footage showing Bhatt wearing gloves and dumping multiple bags into different trash dumpsters. During his testimony, he denied that the bags contained his wife's remains, claiming they held her personal belongings.The prosecution also presented forensic evidence linking blood found on the couple's bedroom carpet to Kafle. A forensic scientist testified that it was "beyond likely" that most of the blood found on the stained carpet belonged to her. Another expert described patterns in the blood evidence that suggested the carpet had been cleaned.Last week, a forensic scientist also testified that DNA and blood samples found on an electric saw were very likely to be Kafle's blood. Prosecutors have said Bhatt purchased the saw months before her disappearance.What is the case against Naresh Bhatt?Mamta Kafle, a nurse originally from Nepal, disappeared from her home in Manassas Park, Virginia, in July 2024. Her body has not been recovered.Bhatt is facing charges of first-degree murder, defiling a dead body and concealing a dead body. He has pleaded not guilty and maintained his innocence.The prosecution had earlier presented testimony from Kafle's brother, Mahesh, who told the court that his sister had shared a photograph appearing to show a black eye and had told him Bhatt was responsible for the injury. He also testified that she had asked him to keep the photograph because she might need it later.A friend of the couple told the court that Bhatt had given her Kafle's jewellery and his wedding ring a few weeks after Kafle went missing. articles.title: 90-year-old Holocaust survivor dies almost a year after being shot in the Sydney Hanukkah massacre
articles.summary: A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor has died almost a year after she was wounded during the massacre of 15 people at a Sydney Hanukkah celebration, officials said Friday.
articles.body: A 90-year-old Holocaust survivor has died almost a year after she was wounded during the massacre of 15 people at a Sydney Hanukkah celebration, officials said Friday. Romanian-born Eva Geller died Thursday night in a Sydney hospital, Executive Council of Australian Jewry director Evan Zlatkis said. She was one of around 40 people wounded when two gunmen allegedly inspired by the Islamic State group opened fire on a crowd at Bondi Beach on Dec. 14. Fifteen victims aged 10 to 87 died. One of the gunmen, Sajid Akram, was shot dead by police at the scene. Rabbi Aron Moss said Geller had been “strong and pretty healthy right up until the Bondi attack where she was shot.” She had been admitted to the hospital several times in recent weeks due to surgery complications, Moss said. “She’s a proud mother, grandmother and great grandmother. A beautiful, positive person who even in these difficult months maintained her positivity,” Moss said on the family’s behalf. “She was told after being shot that she will never walk again by the doctors. But through sheer determination, she got back up and she did walk again,” Moss added. She walked with a cane following the leg wound, he said. The surviving alleged gunman, Naveed Akram, the 25-year-old son of the dead gunman, has been charged with 15 counts of murder, 43 of attempted murder and one of committing a terrorist act. He has yet to enter a plea. It was not yet clear whether Geller’s death would change the charges Akram faces. Police said in a statement they were awaiting advice from a state coroner, who would investigate the circumstances of her death. Akram is scheduled to appear in court next on Feb. 24, when prosecutors expect to finalize what charges will go to the New South Wales state Supreme Court for trial. State Premier Chris Minns offered his condolences to Geller’s family. “After everything Geller endured, the news of her death is heartbreaking,” Minns said in a statement. “Almost a year on, we are still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act. We will never forget Eva or any victim whose life was changed forever,” Minns added. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the devastation of the Bondi attack continued to cause pain for families. “Eva should have been able to celebrate Chanukah (Hanukkah) in peace and safety and instead, her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism,” Albanese said in a statement, using a different spelling of Hanukkah.

articles.title: Macao court sentences pro-democracy ex-politician to 12.5 years in jail
articles.summary: Court finds Au Kam-san guilty of spreading false information and subversion in bid to disrupt Macao’s 2024 elections.
articles.body:
A Macao court has sentenced pro-democracy ex-politician Au Kam-san to 12 years and six months in prison after a closed-door national security trial.

The ruling on Friday found 69-year-old Au guilty of subverting state power by spreading false information in 2023-2024 to disrupt Macao’s 2024 leadership election.

The court said in a statement that Au also worked with “hostile organisations” abroad to spread a political agenda, and leaked confidential information to groups overseas.

“Although the defendant is a first-time offender and admitted to a considerable portion of the criminal facts, he demonstrated a high degree of intent. The degree of unlawfulness and the potential consequences of his crimes are both very serious,” the statement said.

His wife, Virginia Cheang, wrote in a public letter that the case was a political trial and a “groundless” persecution.

“From a closed-door trial to a public verdict, what kind of operation is this? It’s a political trial and it’s a groundless persecution to humiliate one’s character,” Cheang wrote.

Au’s arrest last year was the first public prosecution under Macao’s 2009 security law.

A former teacher, Au sat in the Beijing-dominated legislature for 20 years before resigning in 2021. He also helped organise Macao’s commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protest and massacre in Beijing.

Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director Maya Wang said the sentence sends a chilling message to peaceful critics and called on the European Union and Portugal to push for his release.

Macao’s government and China’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs office all backed the sentence.

This comes a day after Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong , who has been imprisoned since 2020, was jailed for 10 more years under the city’s national security law.

Macao is a former Portuguese colony, which became a special administrative region of China in 1999.

articles.title: ‘Nobody can stop them’: Who are Europe’s Black Bloc protesters?
articles.summary: Anarchistic activists who dress in black and clash with police are a regular feature of protests from France to Albania.
articles.body:
From France and Italy to Spain and Albania, a regular feature of European protest movements has been the presence of a few hundred young people fully dressed in black, often engaged in physical violence with law enforcement.

They have been seen smashing public and private property and setting fire to cars and buildings, and are accused of break-ins and stealing consumer goods – anything from food to jewellery.

Known as the “Black Bloc”, they have aggressive energy that can upend otherwise peaceful demonstrations by student groups and professional unions. While some say they bring attention to social, political, and economic inequalities, others condemn their violent methods, saying they distract from protesters’ legitimate demands.

“The movement started in the 1980s in Germany and came from a social movement called autonomia, or autonomy,” political science professor Francis Dupuis-Deri, at the University of Quebec in Montreal, told Al Jazeera. “They were against the state, capitalism, political parties, even communists and unions. They were more or less anarchists. They believe in living outside the system.”

Dupuis-Deri, who has authored a book on Black Blocs, explained that the anarchists’ idea was “simple”.

“You wear black suits, which was a punk fashion at the time, black leather jackets and cotton hoodies, motorcycle helmets, sunglasses and bandanas. This was a way of making sure they could not be recognised by the police … There is no leadership, no hierarchy, no superstars, no spokesperson, no press statements,” he said.

But he warned against associating the group with any political ideology, left or right, as there have been episodes of right-wing nationalist and neo-Nazi groups in Poland and Germany using Black Bloc attire and violent tactics, although not in recent years.

France has for weeks seen mass student and union demonstrations and is grappling with a high level of violence and property damage.

Al Jazeera contacted the office of a left-wing French member of the European Parliament (MEP), whose party has organised and supported recent nationwide rallies, about the black-clad protesters. But they said the issue was too sensitive to discuss.

“A few cases of violence are used by the government to criminalise our movement and our party, so we don’t want to enter the strategy of speaking about it,” said a person who was not authorised to speak officially on behalf of his elected official.

Italy has also witnessed violence in Rome, Milan, and Turin, with people clashing with police, setting bins and cars on fire, and in some cases causing extensive property damage and injuries.

“Frankly, I’m not aware of any movement inspired by the Black Blocs,” said Mario Furore, an Italian member of the European Parliament from the Five Star Movement. “In Milan, there have been incidents of looting and vandalism, and those responsible appear to have been very young, many of them minors.

“To me, this looks more like copycat behaviour and the influence of bad role models than the work of an organised network. However, it will be up to the judicial authorities investigating the incidents to establish the facts.”

The Black Bloc is not a homogeneous or organised movement with any known leadership or structure. It is also politically somewhat irrelevant because governments and law enforcement groups associate the groups with social protests, whether they are “copycats” or genuine.

Dupuis-Deri said the lack of organisational structure allows members to find each other quickly based on their attire, but they also congregate through word of mouth and form relationships over several demonstrations.

Mobility is a key feature of the movement.

While European governments have not publicised information on the recent demonstrations, Black Blocs are known for having crossed borders in the past to participate in demonstrations in other countries.

“They don’t have a membership roster, so no one really knows how many they are. Intelligence services number them around 5,000-7,000 in Europe, with a few hundred showing up in each demonstration,” said Dupuis-Deri.

Speaking in Parliament in January, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez referenced the group, saying: “Today, at every social demonstration of any significant size, we find Black Blocs who come to smash things and attack the internal security forces.”

A 2023 Italian government document on advanced training for police described the group, its aims, and tactics.

“With the aim of inciting vandalism and violence by infiltrating – and subsequently radicalising – demonstrations, the 1980s also saw the consolidation of a persistent anarcho-insurrectionist tactic: the use of small, loosely organised groups known as the ‘black bloc’,” the document said.

It added that they conduct reconnaissance of target locations well in advance of the planned unrest, dividing these areas into sectors assigned to specific teams, and execute diversionary tactics “carried out by one or more teams to draw the attention of law enforcement away from other groups, which are then free to carry out disruptive or destructive acts”.

The report said the Black Bloc has a “high degree of mobility” to maximise potential damage while minimising the risk of activists being arrested.

Before the recent demonstrations in Europe, perhaps the best-known Black Bloc performances were during the World Trade Organization ministerial meeting in Seattle, the United States, in 1999, and the June 2016 nationwide demonstrations in France against the Loi Travail or labour law.

In both cases, there were confrontations with police, with hundreds injured and arrested.

articles.title: Hoax or bomb threats? What we know about flight disruptions across Europe
articles.summary: Security inspections reveal no explosives as fighter jets escort planes amid Europe’s major wave of bomb threats.
articles.body:
Flights across Europe have been diverted, grounded and escorted by fighter jets in response to a wave of bomb threats, marking a second major outbreak of false alerts in less than a week.

On Thursday, planes departing from 16 countries, including Ireland, the United Kingdom, Spain and Denmark, were affected. Flights have either been forced to divert to alternate locations or undergo additional security checks. On Friday, the threats continued.

Authorities have deployed bomb disposal teams and military fighter jets in several countries. So far, security inspections following threats have yielded no evidence of explosives or suspicious materials on board aircraft, and no passenger has reported being harmed.

On Friday, at least 17 flights had been disrupted by midday GMT.

Hungary said it had scrambled fighter jets three times to escort aircraft through its airspace following bomb alerts received by authorities, including against a WizzAir flight from Brussels to Sofia in Bulgaria, as well as against to flights from Prague to Bucharest and Cyprus.

The Bulgarian transport ministry told AFP it had received alerts about two flights coming in to Sofia.

Prague airport confirmed to media that nine flights had been affected by bomb threats on Friday morning.

A Ryanair flight landed in Lisbon, Portugal at 8am after a bomb threat was made by phone to the authorities, Italian media has reported. A security operation was mounted as soon as the plane landed.

Separately, the control tower in Fiumicino, Italy, received an alert about a device aboard a Wizzair flight to Rome from Paris. The Wizzair flight was diverted to Venice where police were clearing the area around the plane.

On Friday morning, police in Copenhagen, Denmark, said security checks at the airport had found “no danger to passengers”.

On Thursday, there were numerous threats, including the following:

In Poland, authorities received a warning about a potentially dangerous object on board a Polish Airlines flight already taxiing on the runway at Warsaw Chopin Airport. The flight to Paris was prevented from taking off and passengers disembarked, but a search by security services found nothing dangerous on board, an airline spokesman told local media.

In Warsaw, a LOT flight to Paris was also halted and passengers were transferred to another ‌aircraft.

A LOT flight from London Heathrow to Warsaw-Chopin Airport was forced to land at the Polish capital’s other airport, Warsaw-Modlin, following a threat. Nothing was found on board.

The Italian Air Force escorted a Finnair plane into Rome after an anonymous bomb-threat email was sent to Aeroporti di Roma (ADR) and other companies at Fiumicino. The plane arrived safely.

In Bulgaria, a Ryanair flight from London to Sofia was diverted to make an emergency landing in Plovdiv, the country’s second city, following a bomb threat.

In the space of just 20 minutes, Spanish authorities reported receiving three emailed bomb threats regarding two Air Europa departures from Madrid to Paris and four inbound Iberia flights from Rome and Milan, Spain’s Guardia Civil said.

A flight ⁠from Cork in Ireland was delayed for 90 minutes when the airport received a threat, the airport operator said.

A Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Charleroi in Belgium was subject to a false bomb alarm, state news agency Ansa reported. Local media in Belgium reported that security protocols were triggered after the word “bomb” was found written in one of the aircraft’s restrooms.

When an airline is notified of a threat to an aircraft, it is passed to a team of assessors, said Joji Waites, director of flight safety, policy and regulation at BALPA, the British Airlines Pilots’ Association.

“These assessors use standard processes to grade the threat and decide whether the threat is red (credible), amber (partially credible) or green (not credible). Amber is not considered an appropriate assessment if the plane is airborne,” said Waites.

After receiving a threat, an aircraft is directed to an area well away from the airport buildings. Passengers are disembarked and screened while border police with sniffer dogs inspect the plane, according to an airport official.

Is this the first time threats like this have been made?

The incidents follow a series of hoax bomb threats earlier this week. On Monday, a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that turned out to be without substance. On Tuesday, seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted because of malicious hoax bomb alerts.

And also this week, there have also been cyberattacks on supermarkets in several European cities, with hackers changing the temperature on refrigeration in an apparent attempt to spoil food.

Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said the scale and coordinated nature of these latest incidents are unusual.

“There are indeed individual airlines that experience a bomb threat every day, but most of those are very quickly evaluated and determined to be non-specific, and the aircraft do not divert,” said Baum.

What sets the latest incidents apart, he said, is that authorities across several European countries appear to be treating the threats as credible enough to require planes to land and undergo security inspections. Baum noted that each flight disruption could cost airlines as much as $250,000.

The UK’s government called the latest disruption “malicious hoax threats”. London Heathrow, the busiest airport for passenger traffic in Europe, was also targeted. It says it has one of the most robust aviation safety systems in the world, but countries still have to take the threats seriously and figure out how to stop any actors from creating further disruptions to air travel across Europe.

The European Commissioner for Transport said it is too early to say who’s behind these attacks or whether the incidents are even connected.

European governments have so far refrained from blaming anyone. But those which have supported Ukraine are wary of hybrid attacks. Germany has directly pointed the finger at Russia for recent drone incursions at Leipzig-Halle Airport. Moscow rejected the accusations.

EU officials are aware of the possibility that Russia would step up its hybrid campaign. In September, the Danish Defence Intelligence Service warned that this could happen to pressure adversaries in the West and NATO.

However, Moscow has denied being involved in the threats to aviation in Europe and there is no evidence of any involvement by Russia, Iran or any proxy groups linked to them.

articles.title: Rocket launcher deal illustrates deepening Russia-Iran relations
articles.summary: Report of deal comes as top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei discusses developing cooperation treaty with Putin.
articles.body:
Russia has supplied Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers, reports have said, as Moscow confirmed its close relations with Tehran.

Russia agreed a deal in 2024 to supply Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing documents from a major Russian defence manufacturer.

The report came a day after a senior Iranian official visited Moscow to discuss expanding a defence pact signed last year, and illustrates that Russia continues to deepen relations despite seeking the support of the United States for its narrative concerning the war in Ukraine.

The launchers are designed to carry Russia’s light multipurpose guided missile, known as the LMUR or Izdeliye 305. The precision weapon, capable of striking moving targets, entered military service in 2022 and has since been widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine.

The weapons are built for Russia’s Mi-28 attack helicopters, which Iran already possesses. Al Jazeera was not able to confirm if the order has been delivered.

The reported deal illustrates the strengthened military ties between Moscow and Tehran since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Western intelligence officials warn the relationship has further deepened amid the US war in the Middle East, despite President Donald Trump’s recent claims that Moscow was doing “very little, if anything” to help Iran.

The details of the deal emerged a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin met top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei at the Kremlin. Rezaei delivered a message from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during the visit, which was aimed at “further development of bilateral cooperation”, the Kremlin said in a statement released on Friday.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with Putin in late October.

The two countries, both under heavy Western sanctions, have continued to pull closer together in recent years.

In January 2025, they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty covering trade, military cooperation, science, culture, and education.

The treaty took effect in October of that year, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it does not include a mutual defence clause.

However, the deal to supply the helicopter-mounted launchers highlights that military ties continue to strengthen. On Saturday, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Tehran had bought Russian Su-35 fighter jets.

Meanwhile, amid the war in Ukraine, Tehran has provided Moscow with ammunition, artillery shells, firearms, short-range ballistic missiles, helmets, and flak jackets. It was suspected to be supplying drones.

After meeting Putin on Thursday, Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said the talks had focused on security arrangements in the region, as well as Russia’s support for ending what he called the US “aggression” against Iran.

“Important regional issues were discussed with Putin and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements,” Rezaei said.

The Kremlin reported that “further development … of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty” was also discussed.

Analysts suggested to the FT that Russia is walking a fine line to make sure its support of Iran does not disrupt its other relationships, including with other Middle Eastern countries and the US.

“Russia still has certain red lines when it comes to its involvement in this war,” said Hanna Notte at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies. “Which is why the support it has provided to Iran is operationally helpful but is not the game changer in this war.”

articles.title: 1 officer killed and 3 wounded in a firefight with a suspect in Lakewood, Colorado
articles.summary: LAKEWOOD, Colo. — A suburban Denver officer was killed and three others were wounded during a firefight on a transit bus that ended with police fatally shooting the gunman, law enforcement authorities said Friday.
articles.body: LAKEWOOD, Colo. — A suburban Denver officer was killed and three others were wounded during a firefight on a transit bus that ended with police fatally shooting the gunman, law enforcement authorities said Friday. A bystander was also injured. The Lakewood officers had responded to a call Thursday evening about a suspicious person attempting to get on a public bus, police spokesperson John Romero said during a news conference. The person may have been involved in a hit-and-run earlier that day, he said. The man began shooting when officers boarded the Regional Transportation District bus and they fired back, killing the man, authorities said in an update on social media. The three surviving officers were in stable condition at local hospitals, police said. The bystander’s condition wasn’t known, and it wasn’t clear how they were injured. The names of those involved have not been released. “Words cannot express the profound sorrow our department and community feel tonight over the loss of our fallen hero, who made the ultimate sacrifice in service to Lakewood,” the police department posted on social media. “Our hearts are heavy, and we stand shoulder-to-shoulder with their loved ones, lifting them up in unwavering support, love, and prayer during this unimaginable time.” Police said they planned to give another update on Friday. The shootout happened at a busy intersection about 5 miles (8 kilometers) west of downtown Denver. A witness, Teddy O’Brien, told NBC affiliate KUSA-TV that he and several other drivers were stopped next to the bus at a red light when the shooting happened. He said several police cruisers surrounded the bus before officers rushed to it with guns and flashlights drawn. “They hopped on and then shots instantly started ringing from there,” he said. “I instantly just saw shots firing and I ducked down, because you know I’m freaking out at that point.” O’Brien said he saw only one or two people on the bus besides the driver. He said he heard about 30 or 40 gunshots and saw smoke and flashes of light coming from both the front and back of the bus. At a hospital after the shooting, dozens of area police officers gathered outside and a bagpiper played “Amazing Grace” in tribute to the officer who was killed. A long procession of police vehicles then left the hospital. Condolences poured in on social media for the officers and their families. Colorado Gov. Jared Polis ordered all flags to be flown at half-staff on the day of the deceased officer’s memorial, which he said is still to be determined. “Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety every day, and I am heartbroken to learn that a Lakewood Police Agent was killed in the line of duty this evening,” Polis said in a statement. “My thoughts are also with the three agents who are still receiving care at area hospitals, as well as the civilian who was wounded, and I wish them a full and speedy recovery.” Denver Mayor Mike Johnston said police from his city were assisting Lakewood officials. The Regional Transportation District said it is deeply concerned by the shooting and is fully cooperating with police as they conduct their investigation. “Our thoughts are with the victims involved in this tragic incident,” RTD general manager and CEO Debra A. Johnson said in a statement. “RTD is deeply connected to the communities we serve, and events that occur within those communities can at times extend onto the transit system. While this incident is not reflective of the experience we strive to provide, our commitment to delivering a welcoming customer experience remains unwavering.” Colorado State Patrol said in a statement that their hearts are broken over the death of the officer. “To the three additional Lakewood Agents who were injured in tonight’s shooting, we are sending our deepest prayers, strength and best wishes for a full recovery,” the statement said. Patrick Dickman was outside a nearby pawnshop when the shooting unfolded, he told NBC News. Dickman said at about 6:45 p.m., “I was inside the pawn shop, and right there, and it was, like, gunfire started erupting, and then I looked out, and I said, ‘that doesn’t sound good.’” He added that the gunshots sounded “rapid” and he guessed they were coming from an assault rifle or machine gun, he said. “There must have been, like, 700 cop cars down there,” after gunfire rang out, Dickman said, adding that he took cover behind a bus bench to avoid being caught in the crossfire. “I wish it was me instead of the cop that was shot, you know?” Dickman said. “I would take a bullet for any cop any day, you know?”

articles.title: 4 Cornell lawsuit defendants join effort to oust Letitia James from criminal investigation
articles.summary: Four men named in a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit are joining an effort to block New York’s attorney general from leading a reopened criminal investigation into the woman’s gang rape allegations, according to court filings.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Four men named in a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit are joining an effort to block New York’s attorney general from leading a reopened criminal investigation into the woman’s allegations, according to court filings on Thursday. The men agreed to be added to a co-defendant’s court petition seeking Attorney General Letitia James’ removal from the case because of social media posts she made prior to her involvement in which she condemned the alleged assault and expressed support for the accuser. The development comes a day after James appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal prosecutor who oversaw a sex crimes case against music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs, as outside counsel for the investigation. She and a team of lawyers and investigators will be responsible for evidence gathering, witness interviews and other investigative steps. They will report to James. A judge heard arguments last week on one accused man’s request to remove James but said he wouldn’t rule without knowing if the six other lawsuit defendants backed the effort. He gave the man’s lawyers until Thursday to try to get them to join. Four agreed to join, including one whose lawyers had previously filed court papers seeking to have James removed. The two others didn’t have lawyers and did not respond, court filings said. James’ office declined to comment. A former Cornell student identified in court papers as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit in September alleging that several men raped her at a fraternity party in 2024. The woman said some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. Not all of the men named were accused of rape. James, a Democrat, posted about the case on X and Facebook on Sept. 28, linking to a news article about the lawsuit. “I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.” On Oct. 1, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor overseeing the criminal investigation, saying that she had lost faith in the local district attorney, who declined to bring charges in 2024 but had said he would restart the investigation following the former student’s lawsuit. James initially declined to comment about her social media posts but addressed them at an Oct. 8 debate, saying: “Those comments demonstrate empathy, and what we need now more than ever in our body politic is more empathy.” In court, the state’s lawyers argued that Hochul has wide latitude to appoint special prosecutors and said she picked James because of her track record handling sensitive cases in the national spotlight. In a statement on Wednesday, James said she is confident that Kelly “will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.” Andrew Miltenberg, a lawyer for the man spearheading the removal effort, said in a court filing that Kelly’s appointment “changes the face of the investigation” but “does not establish any change in ultimate authority.”

articles.title: Ex-MIT professor wins $6M after sex claims wrecked career, accuser joked about ‘#hetoo’
articles.summary: David Sabatini's $6 million defamation win over Kristin Knouse now faces cross-appeals as both sides prepare to battle in Massachusetts courts.
articles.body: A Massachusetts jury awarded former MIT biologist Dr. David Sabatini a $6 million defamation victory over sexual misconduct claims, setting the stage for cross-appeals as both legal teams prepare to take the case to a higher court. Dr. Kristin Knouse, the former colleague whose sexual misconduct allegations dismantled Sabatini's American academic career, is challenging the October verdict. Her decision triggered a battle over legal consequences surrounding workplace misconduct claims and the authority of campus tribunals. Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zucker, believes that the $6 million verdict could potentially stop female scientists from reporting misconduct, claiming the jury's decision reflects a society that refuses to believe women who challenge powerful men. US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD WINS LEGAL BATTLE AFTER VOLLEYBALL COACH'S $250M DEFAMATION SUIT IS DISMISSED "When someone can get sued for having spoken out, that kills the willingness of anyone to participate in an investigation," Zucker told Fox News Digital. "Daring to speak out will get you sued, [and] the likelihood that anyone would come forward goes down a lot." Sabatini’s legal team rejected the narrative. His attorney, Lisa G. Arrowood, told Fox News Digital that the verdict poses zero threat to genuine victims. "The jury verdict in this case should have no impact on women who truly have been harassed or abused and decide to report the misconduct," Arrowood said. "What the jury found here, based on the contemporaneous documents written by Dr. Knouse herself, was that no harassment ever occurred and that her claims of harassment and rape were false and defamatory. This jury verdict, therefore, has no bearing on people who report truthfully." Arrowood also expressed confidence that the $6 million penalty would withstand appeal. "This is her right," Arrowood said. "However, the judge was very careful in this case and frequently ruled in her favor on many close calls. We think her appeal will be unsuccessful." FORMER CAL SOFTBALL PLAYER FILES LAWSUIT AGAINST UNIVERSITY, FEMALE EX-COACH OVER ALLEGED SEXUAL MISCONDUCT Zucker argued that the verdicts will not stand, warning that penalizing accusers threatens future institutional investigations. "We do not believe the verdicts will stand," Zucker said. "Our client came to court and told the truth about her experiences with Sabatini, as did multiple other women; investigators uncovered several violations of institutional policy." The upcoming appellate fight will scrutinize the events that led to the lawsuit. Consensual or coerced The pair first met in 2012, when Knouse was a doctoral student in the Harvard-MIT M.D./Ph.D. program and Sabatini served on her thesis committee. By 2018 — after Knouse had been named a Whitehead Fellow — they began a relationship, according to court documents. FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL Sabatini maintained the relationship was consensual. Knouse alleged it was coerced and that Sabatini created an inappropriate workplace dynamic. A 2021 Whitehead investigation found Sabatini violated its workplace relationship policy. Text messages made public during the case showed Knouse wrote that she would "fixate on how I’m being held as a backup and competed against other women," Boston 25 News reported. In one message about visiting Sabatini's hotel room one night on a work retreat, she wrote: "In hindsight, it was quite aggressive, #hetoo," according to the outlet. Knouse launched a campaign against Sabatini that she called "Covert Operation Dethrone," Boston 25 reported, and joked in one message about buying a "Lambo" if she won a settlement. "Dr. Sabatini and his legal team do not criticize the MeToo movement or the right of women to complain of harassment," Arrowood added. "This case is unique in that the jury found that Dr. Knouse’s claims were fabricated and designed to cause harm to Dr. Sabatini." After Knouse accused him of sexual misconduct, MIT administrators stripped Sabatini of his tenured position. The Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) dismissed him. The Whitehead Institute ousted him. CBS NEWS FACES $20M DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AFTER MISIDENTIFYING MARYLAND TEENAGER IN REFLECTING POOL REPORT Arrowood said that Sabatini’s team is launching its own counter-offensive on appeal, seeking to overturn the court’s earlier decision that dismissed the Whitehead Institute from the lawsuit. MIT and HHMI were not defendants in the defamation lawsuit. MIT declined to comment but referred Fox News Digital to a letter sent out to staff in 2022, when Sabatini resigned and the school said he was found to have "behaved in ways incompatible with the responsibilities of faculty membership." HHMI did not respond to a request for comment. BIDEN OFFICIALS CIRCUMVENTED COURT ORDER IN TITLE IX CASES, INCLUDING MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS, DOCS SHOW Title IX Investigations The universities based their firings on internal Title IX investigations, which concluded that Sabatini violated policies by entering into an undisclosed romantic relationship with a junior researcher. The campus tribunals require a low burden of proof, which rarely allows the accused to cross-examine the accuser, according to the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. Arrowood argued that the institutions rushed to judgment before the facts could be tested in a civil court. "This verdict should send universities the message that all the facts and documents from both sides need to be obtained and analyzed before deciding to fire someone," she said. SEND US A TIP "Here, the investigators and the Whitehead Institute allowed one party and her lawyers to control what evidence they received and even what they could show to Dr. Sabatini. Had the full picture been shown to the institution and to the investigators, we believe the outcome would have been different." GOT A TIP? When the legal battle reached a Suffolk County courtroom, the jury denied Knouse’s counterclaims of harassment and instead ordered her to pay Sabatini millions for defamation. While Sabatini won the courtroom battle, the years-long ordeal destroyed his U.S. research operation. Activist billionaire Bill Ackman stepped in and funded a new laboratory for Sabatini in Prague, where Sabatini continues his life-saving cancer research. "I've been dreaming about this moment for all this time, but often thinking I might not make it, financially, emotionally or physically." articles.title: STEVE MOORE: After midterm rout, here’s how Trump can start fixing affordability

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING Challenge governors to lower or suspend their gas taxes until prices are back well below $4 a gallon. articles.title: Stocks tumble as midterms fuel AI fears and judge halts Trump’s D.C. arch: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: U.S. markets took a hit as concerns over newly elected Democrats added to fears about AI.
articles.body: U.S. markets took a hit as concerns over newly elected Democrats added to fears about AI. Mississippi voters nervously await the result of nail-biter Senate race. And scientists believe they’re on the brink of a new era in Alzheimer’s prevention. Here’s what to know today. Stocks plunge as blue wave and AI worries crush tech sales The Nasdaq and S&P 500 suffered their worst single-day losses since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs sent markets tumbling, with both indexes losing trillions of dollars in value. The tech-heavy Nasdaq plunged 6.3% yesterday, shedding $2.3 trillion in market value, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, losing $2.8 trillion. Asian markets also plunged after they opened Thursday night. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Two lackluster earnings reports on Wednesday night from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, triggered the sell-off. The plunge is partially tied to a blue wave of victories by anti-AI candidates in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats elected to governorships, attorneys general posts and Congress have pledged to slow or halt AI data center construction. Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about AI has fueled billions of dollars in investments, but questions about whether it will generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months. Trump blamed Democrats for the market slump in a Truth Social post. But, he has said little about Republicans’ election losses since Tuesday, instead signing a proclamation yesterday designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument. Some economists aren’t worried about the stock market dip. Letting some air out of the AI bubble now, they say, could reduce the risk of a full-blown crash later. Read the full story here. Related coverage: Economists expect the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ October jobs report, set to be released this morning, to show 59,000 added roles, up from September’s 29,000. The unemployment rate is projected to remain at 4.2%. Anticipation and optimism in Mississippi’s nail-biter Senate race The Mississippi Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith remained too close to call as of yesterday afternoon. Colom held a lead of just over 1,700 votes, with only 3,600 ballots left to be counted. If Colom wins, he would not only join the ranks of Democrats who flipped long-red Senate seats, but he’d also become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. From the grounds of Jackson State University to the halls of the Masonic Lodge which houses the Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP, voters feel that the state may soon reach a turning point. “Hopefully, it’s a sign of a new day, and hopefully people in Mississippi will start looking at policies and issues rather than skin color in deciding who will be their leaders and representatives,” said 75-year-old Carroll Rhodes. NBC News’ Bracey Harris reports from Jackson about the mood in Mississippi. Colom, however, said he feels like Democrats gave up on voters in Mississippi before the elections were even underway. “Somehow we got in this cycle where they were like, ‘Well, we can’t win, so we’re not going to try,” he said in an interview with NBC News. “First of all, that’s moral — that’s a shame, right?” he said, pointing out that Mississippians have been afflicted by healthcare cuts, tariffs and threats to voting rights. Read more on Colom’s criticism of the Democratic Party. More election news: City Council member Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the race for Los Angeles mayor. Harmeet Dhillon, the Republican attorney who oversaw a massive overhaul of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division that targeted universities and focused on culture war issues, has resigned. For subscribers: How anger, especially toward Trump’s mass deportation policies, helped fuel Latino voter turnout and a historic Democratic shift in Texas. For subscribers: Many Republicans leaned into the “culture wars” on the campaign trail. An unlikely critic, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, said they were “fighting yesterday’s battle.” Construction on Trump’s D.C. arch blocked swiftly after approval A federal judge blocked construction of President Donald Trump’s proposed “Triumphal Arch” hours after a planning commission dominated by Trump appointees approved the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted a temporary restraining order sought by the District of Columbia and Virginia, barring the administration from taking any steps toward the project for 14 days. The Trump administration had said it expected construction to begin immediately. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the controversial arch in an 8-4 vote, with all four opposing votes cast by commissioners not appointed by Trump. The decision followed more than nine hours of public comments, most of which raised concerns about the arch’s impact on Arlington National Cemetery, as well as its height, scale and safety. Why some lawmakers, veterans and others are opposed to the arch. More politics news: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone following a renewed impeachment effort against him. Staff Pick : Are we approaching a new era of Alzheimer’s prevention? Alzheimer’s disease has historically been difficult to detect and even harder to treat. But the past decade has brought remarkable progress, including blood tests that can identify proteins associated with the disease and treatments that help clear them from the brain. Now, scientists believe they’re on the cusp of the next frontier: preventing Alzheimer’s altogether. To shed light on these advancements, our NBC News colleague Sue Kroll opened up about her journey getting tested and treated for early signs of Alzheimer’s in her 50s. After her mother was diagnosed with the disease, Sue noticed that she was struggling to find words or speak in front of groups. A blood test, followed by a brain scan, confirmed the presence of sticky plaques in her brain that are a hallmark of Alzheimer’s. Sue’s situation is unique, since most Alzheimer’s cases are detected late in life when symptoms are more pronounced. And doctors generally don’t recommend blood tests for people without symptoms, even if they have a family history. To Sue, however, her journey represents a vision for the future: Patients would be screened for Alzheimer’s in their 40s and 50s, then manage their disease through a combination of drugs and lifestyle interventions. Doctors think that scenario could become a reality in the next 10 years. — Aria Bendix, health reporter Read All About It LIV Golf said its planning to shut down after discussions with a financial backer failed to produce an agreement. Gov. Gavin Newsom said he plans to commute all 548 death sentences in California, saying he’s opposed to “state-sanctioned killing.” An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, health officials said, marking the state’s first measles-related death in over 30 years and the U.S.’s third measles-related death reported this week. articles.title: MTV Dirty Sanchez star Michael 'Pancho' Locke dies aged 47
articles.summary: Locke starred in Dirty Sanchez as a stuntman and skateboarder called Pancho, and co-owned a clothing brand.
articles.body:
Tributes have been paid to Michael Locke, star of MTV stunt and prank series Dirty Sanchez, who has died aged 47.

Locke, from Port Talbot, known as 'Pancho', starred in the show and later went on to launch the Welsh clothing brand San Portablo .

His Dirty Sanchez co-star Mathew Pritchard said Locke "was the best" and he would "never forget him".

San Portablo, co-owned by Locke, said the TV star was an "absolute Welsh treasure" who "lived an incredible life".

Its post read: "An absolute Welsh treasure and San Portablo King.

"His brilliance we are sure will still shine through far wide high low and across the seven seas.

"He lived an incredible life and lit up the world with his charm.

"Rest in peace brother, your legend will never cease. It will only gain momentum."

In a video Pritchard, from Cardiff, said he was currently climbing Mount Everest in the Himalayas and would dedicate his journey to its base camp to Locke.

"I'm still a little bit in shock," he said.

"My little friend of more than 35 years has left the building.

"We've had some amazing laughs together over the years. I've known him since he was about 14 years old.

"Of course the Sanchez years, travelled all over the world with him, been in some classic messes with him in the past partying. Now he's gone but I'll never forget him."

Fellow Dirty Sanchez star Lee Dainton, writing on social media, said: "When you grow up skating with your friends you're in your own little world.

"You never think about losing anyone from it. In your head those days and the people you shared them with live forever.

"Since hearing the news all those memories have been flooding back.

"I can see Panch, hear the laughter and remember all the best times like it was yesterday. Then it hits me that he's gone and I still can't believe it."

Locke, Pritchard, Dainton and Dan Joyce starred in the cult classic show which ran from 2003 to 2007 on MTV, airing in 64 countries with more than 400 million viewers.

The UK's equivalent to American stunt film series Jackass, Dirty Sanchez started out in Newport and saw the group travel all over the world performing unhinged stunts.

Locke later became co-owner of streetwear brand San Portablo, set up in Port Talbot in 2016 by former Tata steelworker Nigel Hunt.

Locke moved back to Port Talbot in 2018 and was involved in running the brand and its shop in the town.

Hunt described Locke as "a tonic" and "a good man".

"He had an incredible life, his presence was immense. He lit up rooms for 47 years and he will be really missed," he said.

"He was just himself, humble to the end, loved his family."

articles.title: Democrats take back Congress after Republican wipeout: What lies ahead for Trump’s final two years?
articles.summary: \"Today begins the great American comeback,\" House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared after US voters handed Democrats control of both chambers of
articles.body: "Today begins the great American comeback," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared after US voters handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, dealing a major blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.The result marks a dramatic reversal of political fortunes in Washington. Democrats made significant gains in the Senate and House of Representatives, flipping seats in traditionally Republican states, including Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Kansas. They also captured key gubernatorial races, including in Texas and Georgia.Republican candidates struggled even in contests they were widely expected to win comfortably, reflecting growing voter dissatisfaction with the Trump administration. The results represent the first major electoral check on Trump's power since his return to the White House.Discontent over the economy, rising living costs, the war in Iran and the administration's aggressive immigration crackdown emerged as key factors behind the Republican rout.But what does the Democratic takeover mean for Trump? With two years left in his presidency, he still commands the executive branch and retains considerable constitutional powers. Democrats, however, will now control congressional committees, investigations, legislation and Senate confirmations, setting the stage for an increasingly contentious relationship between the White House and Capitol Hill.Trump weakened, but still holds the vetoThe new Congress, the 120th, is scheduled to take office on January 3, 2027. Democrats will then control both chambers for the first time during Trump's current term, giving them a powerful platform to challenge his legislative agenda.The immediate consequence is likely to be a legislative slowdown. With majorities in both chambers, they will have greater authority to direct committees, convene hearings, launch investigations and issue subpoenas, giving them powerful tools to scrutinise the Trump administration.Incoming Democratic leaders have signalled that they intend to examine a range of issues, including the conduct of the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, alleged corporate corruption and the release of the Epstein files.Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to lead a powerful House oversight committee, offered a glimpse of the approach Democrats could adopt, warning those connected to the administration to "lawyer up".The prospect of impeachment could also return to the centre of Washington politics. Democrats will be able to subject Trump's nominees to greater scrutiny, delay confirmation proceedings and potentially reject candidates they oppose.The implications could be particularly significant for the federal judiciary. If vacancies arise on the Supreme Court or in lower federal courts during the remainder of Trump's term, Senate Democrats could block his nominees or press the White House to consider candidates capable of attracting bipartisan support.The shift in Senate control could therefore slow Trump's efforts to fill key positions across the government and limit his ability to shape the federal judiciary in his final two years.From immigration to the Iran war: What issues will Democrats focus on?The war in Iran is likely to become one of the most contentious areas of confrontation between the White House and the new Congress. But it does not automatically translate into a reversal of existing executive orders or regulations.Immigration attorney Bhumireddy Sai Srinivas Reddy told The Times of India that immigration powers are divided between Congress and the president. While Congress makes immigration laws and controls agency funding, the president implements them through executive orders, agency rules and enforcement priorities."Whichever party controls Congress, its main tools are oversight and funding. Congress can hold hearings, request information from DHS and USCIS, and set conditions in agency budgets. But it cannot cancel an executive order or regulation on its own," Reddy said.He added that most day-to-day changes in immigration policy would continue to depend on the executive branch, federal agencies and the courts."For Indian H-1B workers, the near term may bring more policy debate and review, not an automatic change to visa rules. Any major reversal would require legislation, successful legal challenges or changes in executive policy.The next two years could test both partiesThe Democratic victory does not mean Trump has lost control of the presidency. But these, too, could face legal challenges, congressional scrutiny and restrictions through federal spending decisions.The political stakes will extend well beyond immediate legislative battles. The midterm results have effectively opened the contest for the 2028 presidential election, with both parties under pressure to demonstrate that they can respond to voters' concerns.Democrats will have to show that they can do more than oppose Trump. articles.title: Doomsday cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison for 191 murders
articles.summary: MOMBASA, Kenya — The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people.
articles.body: MOMBASA, Kenya — The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people. The High Court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus. Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the “primary criminal culpability” for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death. Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency. On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of the accused guilty of the murder of 191 people. In 2023, more than 400 bodies were exhumed from shallow graves on the 800-acre (320-hectare) Chakama Ranch in coastal Kilifi County, where Mackenzie’s followers lived in mud huts, away from the scrutiny of local communities and authorities. More than 60 bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, while many others remain unidentified and unclaimed. During the sentencing, Kavedza said that 183 victims died of starvation, defined as a complete lack of food, and the other eight were classified as murder by direct homicide. Kavedza said the killings were “cold and calculated” and dismissed claims by some of the accused that the loss of their own children altered the fact that they had participated in the killings of many other children. The justice said that the perpetrators didn’t show remorse and declared they were ready to fast to death as well. During the sentencing, Mackenzie often smiled and chatted with his assistant pastor, Smart Mwakalama, who was sentenced to 160 years in prison. The prosecution had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie and life imprisonment for his accomplices. Mackenzie is also facing terrorism, child abuse and torture charges in two other courts.
