articles.title: US rockets firm could take over mothballed Highland spaceport
articles.summary: Colorado-based Leap is looking at the spaceport near Tongue as its first launch site outside of the US.
articles.body:
A rockets manufacturer says the mothballed Sutherland Spaceport could become its first launch site outside the US.

Colorado-based Leap has agreed to work with Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE), which owns the area of peatland near Tongue, to develop the plans.

Little work has been done at the site after Moray-headquartered rockets firm Orbex put construction on hold in 2024 . The company later collapsed and its assets were sold off .

Leap said the spaceport could potentially be used for launching small satellites for customers in the UK and mainland Europe.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Leap is designing rockets that could be mass produced in factories.

Chief executive Chris Beckman said: "We're not just building a rocket. We're building a global logistics network, and a network needs launch sites wherever customers require them.

"Sutherland is an ideal starting point for a network that begins in Europe, and HIE shares our ambition to make recurring spaceflight from Scotland real."

HIE and Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn have welcomed the agreement.

The site is on Melness Crofters Estate, an area of small-scale farms on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland in the north-west Highlands.

Chairwoman Dorothy Pritchard said the estate was delighted to welcome Leap as a potential launch operator.

She said: "We believe their presence here will be an important step towards establishing a thriving and sustainable spaceport that can bring long-term benefits to Sutherland and the UK's growing space industry.

"Alongside other UK launch sites, both developed and emerging, an operational Sutherland Spaceport will become an integral part of a resilient and diverse UK launch ecosystem, securing the UK position within the global space economy, something we welcome and support.

"Melness Crofters Estate looks forward to seeing the spaceport become a driver of economic opportunity."

Last month, the UK and German governments said they planned to use another Scottish spaceport - SaxaVord in Shetland - as part of increased co-operation between the two countries.

The agreement followed a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week.

In a joint statement, the two governments said they would deepen strategic co-operation on civil, commercial, security and defence interests in space.

SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport and has regulatory approval for up to 30 rocket launches a year.

articles.title: MATT CALKINS: After years of threats and intimidation, the bullies in the women's sports debate finally lost
articles.summary: Riley Gaines and advocates faced years of harassment, but Initiative 638 and Prop 134 passed in deep-blue Washington and Colorado nonetheless.
articles.body: They passed. First, Initiative 638 in Washington. Then, Prop 134 in Colorado. Two measures that will enforce the separation of boys and girls in sports — two measures that show common sense can prevail over partisanship. Many will view these results as a bellwether for where the rest of the country is heading. If policies like these can pass in deep-blue states, proponents will argue they can pass anywhere. WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS But me? I see something else entirely. I see the people finally sticking it to the bullies. Let's go back to July, when Washington high school student Ahnaleigh Wilson attended a rally supporting Fever guard Sophie Cunningham at Climate Pledge Arena. Do you remember what happened inside the venue after the game started? Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton approached Wilson — who was holding a sign reading "Thank You Sophie For Speaking Up For Girls!" — and began cursing her out. "You're f---ing insane," she allegedly said. "I hope Jesus can forgive you." Wilson was brought to tears...but this was hardly a one-off. HOSTILE VALKYRIES FANS VERBALLY ATTACKED WOMEN'S SPORTS ACTIVISTS AT WNBA FINALS GAME 1 IN SAN FRANCISCO Fellow Washingtonian Frances Staudt chose not to play against a male in a high school basketball game over two years ago. Since then, she said she has endured daily harassment at Tumwater High, with people telling her they hope she chokes and dies and goes to hell. Former high school softball star Kendall Kotzmacher may have had it worse. At a Cunningham rally in Minnesota earlier this year, a pro-trans counterprotester told her that she should have been aborted. And don't for a minute think this stops with the kids. XX-XY Athletics founder Jennifer Sey shared a video of her and her friends being called to the concourse to meet with security at a Golden State Valkyries game last month. During their march up the stairs, a woman flipped her the bird and told her to "f---ing kill yourself." But that was just a foreshock to what women's sports advocates endured at a Portland Thorns game two Fridays ago. After a group of about 20 XX-XY supporters unfurled a banner that said "Save Women's Sports," Thorns supporters started yelling "f--- you" before sending one woman tumbling over two rows of seats. They also started poking women with flagpoles they'd brought into the stadium. I saw this up close while reporting for OutKick, but had my phone knocked out of my hand and beer poured on me while filming it. So who got kicked out? Not the assaulters. Nope, it was the peaceful Save Women's Sports crowd — with Seattle-based podcaster Brandi Kruse having her hand restrained behind her back as she was walked up to the concourse. BRANDI KRUSE TELLS LAURA INGRAHAM ABOUT BEING FORCED OUT OF PORTLAND SOCCER GAME: 'WE DID NOTHING WRONG' Even a Lyft driver got in on the hazing, as he booted four XX-XY shirt-wearers from his car once he found out who they were aligned with. The bullies are everywhere. But you know what? They lost. People don't have to be afraid to take a pro female stance on this issue anymore. The outrage mob may try to sink their talons into anyone who does, but they've been declawed by the will of the people — who sliced right through the propaganda. Did you know opponents of Prop 134 outspent the 'yes' campaign nearly 18 to 1—dropping $4.9 million against just $270,000—only to come up empty? Did you see all those ads or newspaper endorsements in Washington claiming that I-638 was going to lead to "invasive genital exams?" Nobody bought it. The two measures sailed through in two of the bluer states in the country. Just less than a month ago, I was at a cross country meet where a boy who switched to the girls team midseason was competing. Out of maybe 100 parents I tried to talk with, just two went on the record — and the vast majority refused to even be quoted anonymously. Said one father: "I don't want my house burned down." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The bullies have been throwing blows on this issue for years now. Just ask advocates such as Riley Gaines, who's been enduring them from every angle. The thing about bullies, though, is they always feel small inside. After these two measures passed, they feel even smaller.

articles.body: A 98-year-old Australian World War II veteran was stunned after a plumber quoted him tens of thousands of dollars to fix a blocked toilet, despite another tradesman later completing the repair in about 20 minutes. John Rose, from Sydney, had turned to Google after his toilet developed a blockage and began making an unusual sound. The plumber who attended told him the job could cost around more than $30,000, a figure Rose initially believed he would have to find the money to pay. He had already spent thousands on the initial plumbing work before a neighbour urged him to seek a second opinion.How a blocked toilet turned into over a $30,000 plumbing billRose's plumbing problem began with what appeared to be a relatively straightforward blocked toilet. The World War II veteran went online to find someone who could investigate the issue, eventually contacting a plumbing company that attended his home. According to A Current Affair, Rose is a trusting person and accepted the plumber's assessment that the problem would require substantial work. The initial diagnosis quickly turned into a much larger financial concern when he was told the repair could cost more than $30,000.98-year-old veteran was left fearing he could not afford the repairThe size of the proposed bill left Rose seriously considering how he would pay for it. The 98-year-old in 2025 said he began working out how much money he had available across his accounts after being told the job could run into the tens of thousands. The situation was particularly concerning because he had sought help for a blocked toilet rather than a major renovation or extensive building project. The plumbing company had already received about $6,000 from Rose by the time his neighbour became involved, according to reporting on the case.Neighbour stepped in after hearing the staggering plumbing quoteRose's neighbour stepped in after hearing about the proposed cost and encouraged him not to proceed without another assessment. That decision dramatically changed the outcome. A second plumber was brought in to inspect the toilet and offered a vastly lower price than the original quote. The replacement plumber ultimately completed the repair in about 20 minutes, showing that the immediate problem could be resolved without the extensive and expensive work Rose had initially been led to expect.Second plumber fixed the toilet in just 20 minutesThe second opinion saved Rose from paying tens of thousands of dollars for the proposed work. The plumber who took over the job was able to fix the toilet in roughly 20 minutes, according to A Current Affair. The stark difference between the two assessments became the central issue in Rose's story, particularly because the original plumber had already charged him thousands of dollars. The case also highlighted the value of obtaining another quote before agreeing to expensive work, especially when a repair is described as urgent or unusually costly.The huge difference between the two plumbing assessmentsThe incident came amid regulatory scrutiny of the plumbing businesses involved. Australian Trades Pty Ltd, which operated under several plumbing names, was subsequently banned for 60 days while authorities investigated complaints about its work and pricing. The action covered businesses including Ferguson's Plumbing, Dan's Plumbing and others operating under the same company. NSW Better Regulation and Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong said authorities could impose financial penalties and suspend or cancel licences if evidence of wrongdoing was established.Why Rose said he would rather give the money to charityThe experience also had a personal financial dimension for Rose, who said he would have preferred to spend the money supporting charitable causes rather than on an unnecessarily expensive plumbing job. His neighbour's intervention meant he avoided the tens of thousands of dollars that had initially been proposed. Rose said he was sharing his experience to warn others about the importance of getting a second opinion when a tradesperson presents an unexpectedly large bill. articles.title: James Carville cautions Democrats to stay away from DEI policies after midterm victories
articles.summary: James Carville warns Democrats against reviving DEI and woke politics after their historic midterm victory, saying the country simply "hated it."
articles.body: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned Democrats against reviving DEI and woke policies after dominating the midterms, arguing these policies hurt the party. Carville spoke with a panel on Thursday’s episode of the "Politics War Room" podcast about the Democrats' midterm victories before responding to a statement from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., declaring that "DEI is back." "I really like him. He's a very personable man. I think these people are all wrong," Carville reacted. "They tried DEI. The country hated it. Just hated it. It cost us seats." Carville agreed with comments from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., dismissing "Woke 1" and argued that returning to those policies would take the party in the wrong direction. CARVILLE SAYS ONE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST'S 'LUNACY OF THE HIGHEST LEVEL' POLICY COULD HAUNT SWING-STATE DEMS "The DEI people asked me to honor your identity above your humanity. I cannot do that. To me, you're a human being first. And if we bring this bulls--- language back, we're going to pay for it," he said. After the 2024 presidential election, Carville warned that the "stench" of woke politics would cling to the party like a foul smell on a shirt. While he said Democrats had made progress since then, he lamented that some were returning to those policies. "We're finally washing the stench of defund the police, communities of color, or every idiotic jacka-- academic word that [they] could think of. And we got rid of it. And AOC is right. Woke one was some crazy s---. Let's all go back and do it," he said. "Let's have progressive taxation. Let's have pluralism in America. Let's get out of Iran. Let's open rural hospitals. Okay, these are things that we can agree on." Carville explained that he is a liberal, not a progressive, and wants to help rural Americans who may feel abandoned by the Democratic Party. "I think rural America is the most forgotten part of America," he said, warning that his fellow Democrats need to be "talking about the problems of rural America or rural hospitals or rural education or rural libraries or anything else." JAMES CARVILLE WARNS FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES 'TOO HARD-HEADED' TO KNOW THEY'RE UNPOPULAR "And I think to the extent that this whole thing strikes people as another coastal people trying to impose something on the rest of the country, and the rest of the country doesn't want this, and now we're talking about bringing it back?" he warned. Democrat Dan Turrentine, a co-host of "The Huddle," told Fox News Digital that Democrats largely abandoned social issues leading up to the midterms and focused on the economy and tackling "corruption." "Not a single new member from a competitive state or district ran on restoring DEI. Quite the contrary, they stayed away from relitigating settled social issues and focused like a laser beam on costs, chaos, and corruption," Turrentine wrote. "Many people on our side are considering running for president and, in an effort to create a spark, will say controversial things to select audiences. articles.title: US midterm results spark fears in Israel over future of two countries' ties
articles.summary: Staunch US support of Israel has been raised as one of the reasons why Republicans performed so badly.
articles.body:
As the US midterm election results rolled in, long-held Israeli assumptions about the transatlantic alliance began to shatter.

"For us in Israel, this will be a generational sea change," wrote one prominent journalist in Israel's biggest-selling newspaper, right-leaning Yedioth Ahronoth. "The [prime minister, Benjamin] Netanyahu government sowed the wind and reaped the tsunami."

Israel's opposition leaders have lined up to blame their prime minister, with one saying the US results showed "just how toxic Netanyahu has become" among both Democrats and Republicans.

The prime minister himself has so far remained silent.

"Israel's political establishment understood intellectually that things have been shifting. They have not understood how much and how quickly," one US official with knowledge of the situation told me.

Israel's relationship with the US was a campaign issue in races across America.

Many Democratic candidates were sharply critical of Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and the costs of the joint US-Israeli war on Iran was a key issue for many voters.

The US president himself blamed the Iran War for the Republican rout – a war that Israel's leader is widely seen as having promoted to him.

And US Vice-President JD Vance cited the US relationship to Israel as one of four key reasons voters had deserted the party, hammering home the message that the relationship is now seen as a political problem by its key ally.

"That might be even worse than what happened in the midterms," Israeli political and security analyst Yaakov Katz told me. "Because the Democrats we knew about, now [Vance] is pointing the finger and saying: 'Our voters want us to change our position on Israel' – and Israelis don't fully understand where this is going."

What the US midterm results mean for the Middle East

The question plaguing Israelis now is what this means for Israel's security and influence.

The sense of staunch US military and diplomatic support had remained unshaken in Israel despite growing anger among US voters, President Donald Trump's public insults to Netanyahu, and differences over Israel's actions in Iran and Lebanon.

Israel's prime minister continually boasted of his closeness to Trump, describing his "true friendship" and "unwavering support".

And just nine months ago, Israelis watched their armed forces wage war on Iran hand in hand with the US military, as the "unprecedented" coordination of the two allies became a daily mantra among military spokespeople and politicians.

So Trump's unexpected statement during a Fox News interview this week that he would stop $3.8bn (3.4bn euros; £2.8bn) in US military aid to Israel two years earlier than planned, caused shock here – not so much for the loss of aid as for what the move said about Israel's status as a diplomatic partner.

Israel's president said the announcement came as "a bolt from the blue".

"Nobody knows anything," was the headline in a report by Yedioth Ahronoth, adding that officials were still struggling to understand whether Trump's remark was serious, two days on.

The Israeli prime minister's office responded to the news several days later, saying that the shift from US aid to partnership showed "the strength and sophistication" of the bilateral relationship.

US military aid is less than 10% of Israel's annual military budget. But Yaakov Katz, author of several books about Israel's defence and security, said Trump's announcement was the tip of a much larger question around future funding, arms sales and joint military projects with Israel. All of this could be slowed or stalled by a Democrat-controlled Congress, even without the two-thirds majority it would need to overrule Trump.

"Everything that Israel used to get in a simpler, easier process will now potentially be much more complicated, and Israel has to be prepared that this is a new reality," he told me.

"Our entire Air Force is American-made military planes, we're dependent on American spare parts and American weapons. The last three years have shown us how dependent we are on American missile-defence systems. [If] those don't show up at the same pace, that's a real difference – that changes your calculation of what you're able to withstand if you go to war."

Katz believes the midterms could also translate into tougher demands on Israel over its actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and a requirement not to undermine an agreement with Iran.

"Something will change in the US-Israeli relationship, but it's a question of scale," said the US official I spoke to, who was not authorized to speak on the record. "It means shifting to [being] willing to criticise Israel when it's warranted, but the bedrock fundamental relationship will still be there."

In an interview on Israeli television, the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee signalled little shift so far in core American positions, including on Israel's occupation of the West Bank, describing the sanctions imposed by other countries as "irrational" and counterproductive.

Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, told another Israeli channel that Trump would be in the White House for the next two years, and that Israel could "feel good" about the US veto in the UN Security Council – something Washington has repeatedly used in the past to block resolutions that target Israel.

"But we have to pay attention to the voices – not only in the Democratic Party but also the Republican Party – criticising Israel," he said. "It will be harder for us."

Questions over its key alliance have come at a particularly sensitive time for Israel, less than two weeks after its own parliamentary elections left neither government nor opposition with a clear majority. Discussions are now taking place with the country's president, who will decide whether Netanyahu or his centrist rival, Gadi Eisenkot, will get the first chance to form a governing coalition.

"Under my leadership, we will renew and deepen that [US] partnership, strengthen the bipartisan foundations that have long sustained it," Eisenkot said in a social media post.

Another member of his opposition bloc, Yair Lapid, said: "What do we do?"

"We go back to the rule that worked for us for seventy years, and which broke in 2015 when Netanyahu went to speak against [US president] Obama in Congress. Israel doesn't choose sides in America. We work with everyone."

Netanyahu's speech to the US Congress in 2015 is seen as a defining moment in Israel's relationship with the US, when the Israeli leader appealed over the head of America's Democratic president to urge Republicans in Congress not to back a nuclear agreement with Iran.

Since then, Netanyahu has increasingly anchored the alliance in Trump's Republican party, even as alienation among Democrats has grown.

The US official I spoke to said that, before the midterms, Netanyahu could have improved the relationship with Washington by getting rid of his two far-right ministers.

"I think everyone understands now it's bigger than [that]," he said.

How much the new tone in transatlantic relations will play into the task of building a new government in Israel is being closely watched.

Some government supporters argue it has increased the need for political stability, and that Netanyahu provides much-needed continuity and a deep knowledge of the US and its leaders.

"We cannot afford to be dragged into endless political disputes and election campaigns," said one opinion writer in Israel's largest-circulation daily, the right-wing Israel Hayom.

Whoever heads Israel's next government, its American ally may demand more than rhetoric.

In the noisy debate around what this will mean for Israel, the silence of its prime minister – once the whisperer of Washington's elite – is perhaps the most telling voice of all.

articles.title: What a Trump-Xi-Putin summit could mean – and what it wouldn’t
articles.summary: A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting at APEC would be a coup for Moscow, analysts say, but Beijing appears lukewarm.
articles.body:
On the sidelines of this month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, an unprecedented three-way meeting between United States President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place.

“China is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing on Wednesday.

“Work is under way to coordinate such a meeting,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday, adding: “We hope that it will be finalised in the coming days.”

Trump has said he is open to three-way talks focused on nuclear weapons. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it,” he told reporters last month.

The three leaders have met separately but have never held formal talks together.

So could the meeting, pencilled in for November 18-19, actually happen, and what would it mean for the rest of the world? Here’s what we know:

What would Russia get out of a three-way meeting with the US and China?

“It is a big event,” Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

He pointed to Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, who he said has described the meeting as a path towards a new Yalta – the 1945 conference where the leaders of the Soviet Union, the US and the United Kingdom shaped the post-war order in Europe.

That allows Moscow to “talk big”, Bratersky said, while putting Ukraine on the sidelines.

Simply being at the table would make Putin “first among equals”, he added, giving him a photo opportunity to show the world that he will be among those deciding the future of Europe’s security architecture after the war in Ukraine.

If the meeting produced results, he said, it would reflect China’s influence on Russia.

“We should take into account that we are dealing with a much weaker US leader after elections,” Bratersky said.

Trump remains in charge of foreign policy, he explained, but will have less leverage if Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in this week’s midterm elections, start sending money to Kyiv.

“A meeting by itself will be a success,” he said. “Putin will be able to sell it at home”.

Whether anything comes of it should become clear within a month or so, Bratersky said, and the meeting could lead to another during the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December.

If nothing is produced before Christmas, he added, “it will be just a photo op.”

Trump wants “a personal, high-drama encounter” that lets him claim he is “dealing with” the other two great powers on his own terms, Inderjeet Parmar, a professor of international politics at City St George’s, University of London, told Al Jazeera.

A three-way meeting would allow Trump to present himself as “the indispensable deal-maker”, Parmar said, talking up potential deals on Ukraine, trade, energy or arms control.

“After the midterms the domestic political need for a foreign policy ‘win’ is real,” he said.

Any image of Trump sitting with Xi and Putin could be spun as evidence that American power still commands the table, he said, “even if the substance is limited or largely symbolic”.

“The domestic audience, and his eroding MAGA base, matters at least as much as the diplomatic one,” Parmar said.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said he raised the idea of discussing Ukraine with Xi when they met in Beijing on October 30, and could see the “surprise” on his face, Germany’s DPA news agency reported.

Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi said the three presidents would probably meet in Shenzhen, but not to discuss Ukraine.

He said Xi explicitly pointed out that the Russia-Ukraine war is a European conflict in which the “Europeans must sit at the table”.

Beijing is also likely to swat away Trump’s push for nuclear talks.

Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.

What would a meeting mean for the rest of the world?

Parmar said a three-way meeting would mark “a clear break from the post-1945 pattern”, in which Washington coordinated closely with its European and Asian allies before engaging with Moscow or Beijing.

“A free-standing trilateral [meeting] risks treating those allies as secondary players whose interests can be managed after the fact,” he said, adding that those interests could even be traded.

That would be a shift towards “personalised great-power diplomacy”, he said. But the Trump administration still has hopes to drive a wedge between Russia and China, Parmar added.

Fears of a “G3” are “understandable but overstated in institutional terms”, he said, because the three capitals’ interests diverge sharply on Ukraine, Taiwan, technology and the rules of the international economy.

“The real risk is not a formal G3 secretariat, but the normalisation of great-power deals struck with little consultation of those most affected,” he said.

“History offers many examples of such moments. They rarely produce stable order and often leave the excluded feeling the costs,” Parmar said.

articles.title: Burnham says he was not aware of Brand's 'horrific' crimes
articles.summary: The prime minister told the BBC that Labour politicians courting the comedian a decade ago had not been aware of his crimes.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.

Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.

Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

Speaking on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

In 2014, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.

At the time, Burnam said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".

The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.

"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."

The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."

Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.

During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to the same court on Monday for sentencing.

articles.title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
articles.summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
articles.body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have started to climb following an enormous sell-off on Thursday that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

The Nasdaq Composite opened up 1.23% and continued to gain in early trading, reversing some of its 5.5% fall from Thursday.

The S&P 500 - home of the largest publicly-traded US companies that are not in the technology sector - also opened up slightly, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down.

Firms that experienced heavy losses on Thursday also began to bounce back in early trading.

Nvida, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday trading up more than 6%.

SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 7% and nearly 3% respectively.

The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

The increase in jobs was led by the professional and business services sector, which added 70,000 jobs. The healthcare sector added 42,000 jobs, and jobs were also added in transportation and warehousing as well as manufacturing.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title: Claims of a Ukrainian ‘torture chamber’ went viral. What really happened?
articles.summary: A woman who claimed that men were being violently assaulted in a house for evading the draft has been arrested.
articles.body:
Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka, Ukraine – A woman wearing a crisp new paramedic’s uniform and impeccable makeup kneels on the ground in front of several police officers guarding the rusty gates of a two-storey house.

She begs, yells and curses, claiming that forcibly conscripted men are being held in the building in the tranquil suburb of Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka, outside the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv.

One of the men has already died, claims the woman, who was later identified as Valentyna Moloda, a 49-year-old nurse who once worked at a plastic surgery clinic and has never been authorised to practise as a paramedic.

The ambulance she arrived in carries the logos of a private medical company that reportedly stopped operating in 2023. A woman from Moloda’s “ambulance team” livestreams the scene as a crowd swells, joining in her chants demanding access to what she calls a “torture chamber.”

“I’m on my knees, let me get to them,” Moloda screams, claiming that “armed people” allegedly “torture” 40 people inside who had evaded the draft.

Her claims resonate with people at the impromptu rally, in a country where conscription officers have become reviled public servants due to their sometimes brutal tactics.

Protesters lob eggs at police and throw tomatoes at the house. The crowd grows to 500 people, with many clashing with officers until midnight.

Officials say that Moloda’s “rescue mission” on Monday afternoon – one of the most polarising scandals in Ukraine – was fake and required preparation.

But it had already gone viral online, with tens of thousands of people around the world lamenting Ukraine’s handling of conscription.

Glenn Diesen, a pro-Kremlin political analyst from Norway, shared a video and a photo on X of a teenager who fell while trying to film the house from the fence, claiming the boy was a victim of “great outrage and riots in Ukraine against the henchmen of [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy and NATO.” His post has been widely shared.

Three days before Monday’s incident, Moloda and her driver “conducted a reconnaissance” of the house, Ukraine’s Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov said on Tuesday.

A former top military intelligence officer and one of Ukraine’s most popular and trusted public figures, Budanov interacted with Moloda at the time of the standoff.

Several young men clashed with police and tried to kick the doors of the house open until officers let Moloda and her team inside.

She came back minutes later to proclaim that she had just seen a man on the brink of death, another with a broken spine and one who was so badly beaten he was unable to talk.

“There’s blood on the mattresses,” she yelled, showing someone photos of the alleged victims on her phone, while the scene was livestreamed. “They [urinate] in a bottle.”

But careful observers would have noticed the videos were tagged as having been shot on Saturday. The crowd, however, kept growing, damaging police cars and clashing with officers.

Budanov arrived about six hours after Moloda started her livestream, and said that the besieged house on Solnichna Street had been used by the Azov Brigade , a former volunteer militia group of far-right nationalists and football fans that helped repel pro-Russian separatists in southeastern Ukraine in 2014.

Azov said apprehended deserters were kept in the house, while Azov’s commander Denys Prokopenko called the scandal a “sabotage behind the lines that discredits Ukrainian servicemen and creates a narrative that benefits Russia”.

The group has been accused of neo-Nazi sympathies and torturing war prisoners. The United States Department of State banned it from using US-supplied weaponry between 2014 and 2024, but it grew into a military force and became part of Ukraine’s National Guard. Its founder, Andriy Biletsky, led this year’s “Operation Vivaldi” to push Russian forces out of several strategic areas in eastern Ukraine.

After Budanov’s arrival, four men were allowed to walk out of the house into a bus, including the one Moloda claimed could not move because of a broken spine. The angry crowd did not allow the bus to leave.

‘Unfortunately, people believed that woman’

Al Jazeera visited Petropavlivska-Borshchagivka and talked to more than a dozen residents, who insisted on full or partial anonymity because Monday’s scandal has become so politicised.

“Both sides are wrong,” an elderly man who only gave his first name, Serhiy, told Al Jazeera, standing next to his wife outside a supermarket.

“Azov shouldn’t have kept their people there, and the fake doctor shouldn’t have started all this noise,” he said.

His wife signalled him to stop talking and ushered him away.

Locals laughed off comparisons some have made between Monday’s incident and the massive 2013-2014 protests on Maidan Square in central Kyiv that toppled pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanykovych.

“This definitely wasn’t a mini-Maidan,” 17-year-old Mykola told Al Jazeera, a short distance from the house. “Unfortunately, people believed that woman and flocked here.”

Most of the locals called the incident a “provocation”.

Only one man in his 30s said that Moloda “tried to help” and should not have been apprehended on Tuesday.

Moloda was arrested and is being held in custody for 60 days without bail.

Prosecutors said they found evidence proving that she had at least once carried out “rescue services” as a fake paramedic for 107,000 hryvnia ($2,355).

The relatives of a deserter, Andriy Kuleshov, allegedly hired Moloda for about $7,000 to get him out of the Azov house, Pavlo Kurchenko, a senior Azov officer, told the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

Kuleshov is listed in Myrotvorets – Ukrainian for “peacemaker” – a controversial online database of alleged anti-Ukrainian figures, for crossing into separatist-controlled areas in southeastern Ukraine multiple times in 2015-2021, where his brother lives.

“[Moloda] wanted to create a political scandal,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “She is also suspected of ties to Russian intelligence. So far, there’s no confirmation of that, but Russia has used this scandal in its interests.”

It did – with the help of pro-Russia Ukrainians.

“People are being kidnapped and tortured. Some are sold to military units, others – to their relatives. The weaker ones simply die of torture and confinement conditions,” Artyom Dmitruk, a former Ukrainian lawmaker with a pro-Russian party who fled for Italy in 2024, said in televised remarks.

The scandal “answers the question about why Russia needs the special military operation, to uproot the resurgent neo-Nazism in Ukraine,” said Mikhail Sheremev, a “lawmaker” in Russia-annexed Crimea.

Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion prompted a wave of volunteers to join Ukraine’s military, with tens of thousands enlisting across the country, often travelling to other regions because conscription offices near their homes were overwhelmed.

But after heavy losses and reports of poor planning, corruption and the cruelty of some officers, the number of volunteers fell dramatically.

Since 2023, conscription officers have been combing public places in search of people trying to avoid the draft. They have frequently forced them into their vans, often resorting to intimidation, beatings and torture, as Al Jazeera has reported , along with witnesses and human rights groups.

The officers claim there is no other way to mobilise the tens of thousands of men needed on the frontline to repel Russian forces.

The violence has led to corrupt practices.

As of August this year, 76 conscription officers had been arrested for accepting bribes of up to tens of thousands of dollars, stashing huge sums, and buying expensive properties in Ukraine and abroad.

Some draft-dodgers have secured fake exemptions from medical doctors, while others fled to neighbouring countries, either through bribes or by crossing the border without documentation.

Some forcibly drafted men secured the services of “fake ambulances”, according to prosecutors and police.

In 2025, border guards in the southwestern region of Zakarpattia detained a fake ambulance crew of three men who tried to take a person evading the draft to Romania for $10,000.

articles.title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
articles.summary: Ian Winter allegedly confronted a reporter outside court who had investigated the comedian.
articles.body:
Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".

"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin added.

In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".

The journalist claimed that Winter also said to her "well it wasn't you" and swore at her.

On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.

The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."

Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Channel 4 Dispatches, Sunday Times and Times programme.

Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.

Brand is also being investigated over two more rape allegations made by two other women.

Court documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court, held before Brand's criminal trial, suggest one of the women was 16 at the time of the alleged offence and appeared in a Channel 4 documentary. Brand has denied the allegations.

None of the women involved in the media investigation were complainants in Brand's criminal trial.

articles.title: BMC destroys 200kg unsafe food items, fines 13 establishments ahead of Diwali
articles.summary: Bhubaneswar BMC seized and destroyed 200kg unsafe food items, including 160kg sweets, fining 13 establishments Rs 26,500 ahead of Diwali inspections.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Intensifying its crackdown on unsafe food items, especially sweets, ahead of Diwali, Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation’s (BMC) food safety wing on Friday seized and destroyed 200kg of substandard food items, including 160kg of sweets, at various hotels, restaurants and stalls across the city.A total fine of Rs 26,500 was imposed on 13 establishments for various violations.Six food safety teams have been carrying out surprise inspections over the last two days to check the quality and hygiene standards of sweets and other food items, which see high demand during the festive season.Officials inspected 27 establishments, including e-commerce-linked food businesses, at key commercial areas like Fire Station Square, Baramunda, Dumduma, Patia and KIIT Square. During the raids, 24 food samples were collected and sent for laboratory testing.Designated food safety officer Satyajit Patel said the teams detected multiple violations, including improper storage, sale of stale food, use of artificial colours and sweeteners and unauthorised food additives.“Sweet shops and food establishments that are preparing products in unhygienic conditions with poor packaging and storage practices are under the scanner. During inspections, several shops were found keeping sweets uncovered in trays on the ground. In some places, staff were packing food without wearing gloves and working in unhygienic surroundings,” Patel said.Patel said strict action would follow against offenders once the test reports are received. Despite repeated awareness campaigns, some businesses continue to sell stale sweets and use unauthorised ingredients.The enforcement teams also focused on identifying the use of chemical-based artificial colours used to enhance the appearance of sweets.
